question: How does chunk size affect retrieval quality?

frames.data: data: {"type":"block","block":{"type":"CitedSummary","id":"turn-5fd8ab681d59","meta":{"status":"ready","error":null},"data":{"segments":[{"text":"Larger chunks tend to raise recall in evidence retrieval because they are more likely to contain evidence sentences. They also lower precision because they include more irrelevant sentences and add noise.","citationIds":["c1"]},{"text":"The same pattern appears across chunkers. For the clustering-based and breakpoint-based chunkers, larger chunks lower precision in both retrieval tasks, while recall rises sharply for evidence retrieval.","citationIds":["c2"]},{"text":"The extreme case is \"No Chunker\", which treats whole documents as single chunks. It has the highest recall and lowest precision.","citationIds":["c1"]},{"text":"Smaller chunks reduce the number of sentences retrieved, which lowers the chance of retrieving evidence sentences and sharply cuts recall. The F1 score stays relatively unchanged.","citationIds":["c3"]},{"text":"For document retrieval, smaller chunks have little effect on recall, but precision rises significantly. Smaller chunks from the same document are retrieved, so fewer distinct documents are returned.","citationIds":["c4"]},{"text":"Larger chunks are often less desirable because they introduce more noise.
